moduleTitle: SQE1 · Wills and Administration of Estates
title: Family provision claims I: who can claim and what they can claim
subtitle: The eligible applicant categories under the 1975 Act, and the different standards each one is held to
objectives: List the categories of person eligible to apply for family provision under s 1 Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975
Explain the two-year cohabitation requirement and what counts as being 'treated as a child of the family'
Distinguish the spousal standard of reasonable financial provision from the maintenance-only standard applied to every other category of applicant

leadingAuthorities.citation: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, s 1
leadingAuthorities.role: Defines the categories of eligible applicant and the applicable standard of provision

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: A will can be perfectly validly executed and still leave someone out who the law thinks should not have been left out — but only if that person fits inside one of six carefully defined categories. Get the category wrong on the SQE1 and the whole analysis collapses before you reach the merits.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You can name the six categories — the pool below will push you to place borderline people (a fiancé, a lodger, a stepchild) into the right box or the right exclusion, which is where these questions are actually won or lost.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Go through Part 2 slowly and fix all six categories in order before moving on — everything else in this lesson assumes you can list them without prompting.

overview.hook: A will can dispose of an entire estate to a stranger and be entirely valid — testamentary freedom in England and Wales is real, not a formality. And yet a spouse, a child, or even someone who was never married to the deceased at all can sometimes override it. The 1975 Act doesn't rewrite the will; it builds a narrow, carefully policed exception around it. This lesson is about who gets through the door before any court considers the merits.

parts.heading: Testamentary freedom, and the exception carved out of it
parts.voice: argumentative — states the strong default before introducing the qualification
body: English law starts from a firm principle: a testator can leave their estate to whomever they choose, and can cut out a spouse, a child, or anyone else, for any reason or none. There is no forced heirship, no fixed reserved share, and no general legal or moral duty to provide for family members on death.

The Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 is the statutory exception to that freedom — and it is genuinely an exception, not a rewriting of the rule. It allows certain defined categories of person to apply to the court where a will (or the intestacy rules, or a combination of both) fails to make reasonable financial provision for them. It does not allow just anyone who feels hard done by to challenge a will; eligibility is gated tightly by s 1.

This lesson is entirely about that gate: who counts as an eligible applicant. The next lesson in this pathway deals with what the court does once someone is through the gate — the discretionary factors it weighs. Keep the two separate in your head, because SQE1 questions often test eligibility and merits as if they were the same enquiry, and they are not.

components.definition: The statutory standard the 1975 Act applies where a will or the intestacy rules leaves an eligible applicant without adequate financial support — defined differently depending on which category of applicant is claiming.

interaction.prompt: Name the Act that allows certain family members and dependants to apply to court for provision from an estate, even against the terms of a valid will.
acceptableAnswers: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975
Inheritance Provision for Family and Dependants Act 1975
interaction.modelAnswer: The Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 — a narrow statutory exception to testamentary freedom, available only to defined categories of eligible applicant under s 1.

parts.heading: The six categories under section 1
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Section 1 lists exactly who can apply. Learn these as a fixed checklist rather than a general impression of 'close family' — the boundaries are precise and SQE1 tests the edges of each one.

The categories are: (a) the spouse or civil partner of the deceased; (b) a former spouse or former civil partner who has not remarried or formed a new civil partnership; (ba) a person who lived with the deceased as if they were a spouse or civil partner for the whole of the two years immediately before the death; (c) a child of the deceased; (d) any person (not being a child of the deceased) who was treated by the deceased as a child of the family in relation to a marriage or civil partnership the deceased was party to; and (e) any other person who was being maintained, wholly or partly, by the deceased immediately before the death.

Two categories cause the most trouble. The cohabitant category (ba) requires living together 'as' a spouse or civil partner for a continuous two-year period ending on death — a couple together for eighteen months, or together for three years with a six-month separation in the middle, both fail on the facts. And category (d) is not limited to stepchildren of a marriage still subsisting at death — it also catches someone treated as a child of the family within a marriage that had already ended, so long as the deceased was a party to that marriage or civil partnership at the relevant time.

components.label: The six eligible applicant categories — s 1(1) 1975 Act
points: (a) Spouse or civil partner of the deceased
(b) Former spouse or civil partner who has not remarried or formed a new civil partnership
(ba) A cohabitant living as spouse/civil partner for the whole of the 2 years before death
(d) A person treated as a child of the family in relation to a marriage/civil partnership the deceased was party to
(e) Any other person maintained, wholly or partly, by the deceased immediately before death

interaction.prompt: Priya lived with the deceased in a relationship 'as' partners, but they separated for eight months roughly a year before his death before getting back together for the final four months. Is Priya an eligible applicant under category (ba)?
options: No — the two years of cohabitation immediately before death must be continuous, and the separation breaks it
Yes — the total time they were together over the relationship's life exceeds two years
Yes — any cohabitation at the date of death satisfies category (ba)
No — category (ba) requires marriage, not cohabitation
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The requirement is unbroken cohabitation for the whole of the two years immediately before death — a gap of any real length inside that window defeats the category, whatever the relationship's total duration.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The statute asks for the whole of the two years immediately before death, without a break. An eight-month separation inside that window means Priya cannot satisfy category (ba), however long the relationship lasted overall.

parts.heading: The child and family categories, unpacked
parts.voice: case-narrative — uses a worked scenario before the doctrine
body: Category (c) — a child of the deceased — is broader than it first sounds. It includes adult children of any age, not just minors, and it includes children born outside marriage and adopted children. There is no upper age limit and no requirement of financial dependence to be eligible in the first place (though, as the next lesson covers, an independent adult child faces a much harder task on the merits).

Category (d) is different in kind: it is not about biological or adoptive parentage at all, but about being treated as a child of the family. A stepchild the deceased raised as their own, within a marriage or civil partnership the deceased was party to, fits squarely within (d) even with no blood or adoptive tie whatsoever. The category does not require the marriage to be still subsisting when the deceased died — someone treated as a child of the family in an earlier marriage that ended in divorce can still qualify, provided the deceased was a party to that marriage.

Category (e) exists to catch dependants who fall outside every family-shaped box — a long-term lodger the deceased supported financially without any romantic relationship, for instance, or a relative outside the immediate family whom the deceased maintained. The touchstone is maintenance 'immediately before' death: it looks at the practical financial reality at the relevant time, not at family status.

components.definition: Under s 1(1)(d), a person (other than the deceased's own child) treated by the deceased as a child in relation to a marriage or civil partnership the deceased was a party to — typically a stepchild, whether or not that marriage was still subsisting at the deceased's death.

interaction.prompt: The deceased married Grace, who had a young daughter, Nia, from a previous relationship. The deceased raised Nia as his own throughout the marriage. He and Grace later divorced, and the deceased died some years afterwards without remarrying. Is Nia an eligible applicant?
options: Yes — under category (d), as she was treated as a child of the family in a marriage the deceased was party to
No — category (d) only applies while the marriage is still subsisting at death
No — Nia would need to be adopted by the deceased to qualify under any category
Yes, but only under category (e) as a dependant, not category (d)
interaction.explanation: Category (d) does not require the marriage to still exist at the date of death. Nia was treated as a child of the family within a marriage the deceased was a party to, which is enough — the later divorce does not remove her eligibility.

parts.heading: One standard for spouses, another for everyone else
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the puzzle before resolving it
body: Here's the question worth sitting with before the answer is given: if two applicants both show the deceased failed to provide for them adequately, should the court measure their claims the same way? The 1975 Act says no — and the difference is one of the most heavily tested points in this whole area.

For a spouse or civil partner (category (a), and in some circumstances a former spouse under (b)), the standard is 'reasonable financial provision' in the fullest sense: such provision as it would be reasonable in all the circumstances for the applicant to receive, whether or not that provision is required for their maintenance. This mirrors, broadly, what a spouse might have expected on a divorce — provision can go beyond bare maintenance.

For every other category — former spouse under the ordinary rule, cohabitant, child, child of the family, and dependant — the standard is lower: such financial provision as it would be reasonable for the applicant to receive for their maintenance. 'Maintenance' is not generous; it means provision to meet the applicant's reasonable everyday living needs, not provision to enhance their general standard of living or to reward them for the relationship.

components.title: Which standard applies?
components.description: A decision path for identifying the standard of provision that applies to a given applicant.

nodes.label: Is the applicant a surviving spouse or civil partner (category (a))?
Yes → full 'reasonable financial provision' standard — not limited to maintenance
No → which other category applies: (b), (ba), (c), (d), or (e)?

components.textAlternative: First ask whether the applicant is a surviving spouse or civil partner. If so, the full 'reasonable financial provision' standard applies, which is not limited to maintenance. If not, identify which of the remaining categories — former spouse, cohabitant, child, child of the family, or dependant — applies; every one of those is held to the lower, maintenance-only standard.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a surviving spouse's claim under the 1975 Act is limited to what they need for maintenance, in the same way as a cohabitant's claim?
sliderLabels: Definitely limited to maintenance, same as a cohabitant
interaction.explanation: A surviving spouse or civil partner is held to the fuller 'reasonable financial provision' standard, which is expressly not confined to maintenance. Every other category, including a cohabitant, is limited to maintenance.

parts.heading: Reading a claim: which category, which standard
parts.voice: direct — sets up the two-step check the tests will probe
body: In practice, every 1975 Act problem question resolves into the same two-step check before you get anywhere near the merits: first, does this person fit inside one of the six categories in s 1(1)? Second, once you know which category, which standard of provision applies to them — the fuller spousal standard, or maintenance only?

It's worth being explicit about who is very commonly left out. A friend, however close, who was neither maintained by the deceased nor treated as a child of the family, has no claim at all — however unfair the will might seem. Similarly, a fiancé(e) who was never married and never lived with the deceased for the required two-year period does not qualify under (ba), however imminent the wedding was.

The highlighted passage below is drawn from s 1(2) of the Act, which supplies the statutory wording for both standards side by side — the difference in language is small, and that is exactly why it rewards being read closely rather than remembered as a vague impression.

components.citation: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, s 1(2)
components.text: (a) in the case of an application by the wife or husband of the deceased... 'reasonable financial provision' means such financial provision as it would be reasonable in all the circumstances of the case for a wife or husband to receive, whether or not that provision is required for his or her maintenance; (b) in the case of any other application... 'reasonable financial provision' means such financial provision as it would be reasonable in all the circumstances of the case for the applicant to receive for his or her maintenance.
elements: Spousal standard: reasonable provision, not limited to maintenance
All other categories: reasonable provision limited to maintenance

interaction.prompt: In the statutory passage below, highlight the phrase that marks the key difference between the spousal standard and the maintenance-only standard.
interaction.passage: In the case of an application by the wife or husband of the deceased, reasonable financial provision means such provision as it would be reasonable to receive, whether or not that provision is required for his or her maintenance. In the case of any other application, reasonable financial provision means such provision as it would be reasonable for the applicant to receive for his or her maintenance.
interaction.ratioSentence: whether or not that provision is required for his or her maintenance

testPool.prompt: A client asks whether an adult child of the deceased, aged 45 and financially independent, can apply under the 1975 Act. What should the solicitor advise about eligibility alone?
options: Yes — there is no age limit or dependency requirement for eligibility under category (c)
No — only minor children are eligible applicants
No — the child must show financial dependence on the deceased to be eligible at all
Yes, but only if the child was named as a beneficiary in an earlier will
testPool.explanation: Category (c) has no age limit and no dependency threshold for eligibility itself. Independence and age go to the merits of the claim, not to whether the child can apply in the first place.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is a correct statement of category (ba) under s 1(1A) of the 1975 Act?
options: A person who lived with the deceased as spouse or civil partner for the whole of the two years immediately before death
A person who was engaged to marry the deceased at the date of death
A person who lived with the deceased for at least six months at any point during the relationship
A person who cohabited with the deceased for two years at any time before death, whether or not immediately before it
testPool.explanation: Category (ba) requires continuous cohabitation as spouse or civil partner for the whole of the two years immediately before the deceased's death — not any two-year period, and not mere engagement.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor is explaining the difference between the spousal standard and the maintenance-only standard to a trainee. Which statement correctly captures the difference?
options: The spousal standard is not limited to maintenance; every other category's standard is limited to maintenance
Both standards are identical in substance, only the wording differs
The maintenance-only standard is more generous, since it focuses on need rather than fairness
The spousal standard only applies where the marriage lasted more than five years
testPool.explanation: This is the central distinction in s 1(2): a spouse or civil partner can be awarded reasonable provision beyond bare maintenance, while every other eligible category is confined to what is reasonable for their maintenance.

testPool.prompt: The deceased's former wife divorced him eight years before his death and has not remarried. Is she a potential applicant under the 1975 Act?
options: Yes, potentially — under category (b), as a former spouse who has not remarried
No — divorce permanently removes eligibility to apply
Yes, but only under category (e) as a maintained dependant
No — category (b) requires the divorce to have occurred within the last two years
testPool.explanation: A former spouse who has not remarried or formed a new civil partnership remains eligible under category (b), regardless of how long ago the divorce took place.

testPool.prompt: A trainee suggests that a stepchild can only apply under the 1975 Act if the deceased legally adopted them. Is this correct?
options: No — category (d) applies where the deceased treated the person as a child of the family, with no adoption required
Yes — adoption is required for any child-based category
No — but only if the stepchild was under 18 at the date of death
Yes, unless the stepchild was also maintained financially by the deceased
testPool.trapExplanation: It's natural to assume a formal legal relationship is required, but category (d) is deliberately built around the deceased's actual conduct — treating someone as a child of the family — rather than any adoption or blood tie.

testPool.prompt: The deceased's close friend of thirty years, who never lived with him and received no financial support from him, is left out of his will entirely. Can the friend apply under the 1975 Act?
options: No — friendship alone, without maintenance or a qualifying family relationship, does not fit any of the six categories
Yes — under category (e), because of the length and closeness of the friendship
Yes — under category (d), as a person treated like family
No, but only because the friend did not attend the funeral
testPool.trapExplanation: Closeness and duration of a relationship feel like they should matter, but the Act is not a general fairness jurisdiction — without either a qualifying family status or actual maintenance by the deceased, even a decades-long friendship falls outside every category.

testPool.prompt: A couple lived together as partners for one year and eight months before the deceased's sudden death; they had been planning to marry the following spring. Can the survivor apply under category (ba)?
options: No — category (ba) requires the whole of the two years immediately before death, and one year eight months falls short
Yes — the intention to marry satisfies the category even without two years' cohabitation
Yes — any period of cohabitation over one year is sufficient
No — category (ba) requires formal marriage, not mere cohabitation
testPool.trapExplanation: An imminent wedding feels like it should count for something, but category (ba) turns on a strict, unbending two-year cohabitation period ending at death — intentions and near-misses do not satisfy it.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following, without more, is sufficient on its own to make someone an eligible applicant under s 1(1)(e) of the 1975 Act?
options: Being maintained, wholly or partly, by the deceased immediately before death
Being distantly related to the deceased by blood
Having lived in the same house as the deceased at any point
Having been named as a beneficiary in an earlier, revoked will
testPool.trapExplanation: Blood relationship and past cohabitation feel relevant, but category (e) is defined purely by actual maintenance immediately before death — a distant relative who received no support does not qualify under it, while an unrelated person who was maintained does.

testPool.prompt: The deceased's adult stepson, Callum, was treated as a child of the family throughout the deceased's marriage to Callum's mother. The marriage ended in divorce fifteen years before the deceased's death, and the deceased never remarried. Is Callum an eligible applicant?
options: Yes — category (d) does not require the marriage to be subsisting at death
No — the divorce ends Callum's eligibility permanently
No — category (d) only covers minors at the date the marriage ended
Yes, but only under category (c) as though he were a biological child
testPool.explanation: Category (d) looks at whether the deceased treated the applicant as a child of the family in relation to a marriage the deceased was party to — it is satisfied even though that marriage later ended, and even though Callum is now an adult.

testPool.prompt: A cohabitant, Femi, lived with the deceased continuously as partners for exactly two years and one month up to the date of death. Is Femi eligible under category (ba)?
options: Yes — the continuous cohabitation satisfies the whole of the required two-year period ending in death
No — the relationship must have lasted exactly two years, no more and no less
No — Femi needed to be named in the deceased's will to qualify
Yes, but only under category (e), not category (ba)
testPool.explanation: The requirement is cohabitation for at least the whole of the two years immediately before death; exceeding that minimum by a further month does not disqualify Femi — the two-year period is comfortably covered.

testPool.prompt: A surviving civil partner and a maintained elderly aunt (category (e)) both bring claims under the 1975 Act against the same estate. How does the standard of provision differ between them?
options: The civil partner's claim is measured by full reasonable provision, not limited to maintenance; the aunt's claim is limited to maintenance
Both are measured by the same reasonable provision standard, not limited to maintenance
The aunt's claim is measured more generously, since she is not a family member by right
Neither claim is limited to maintenance, since both are named categories under s 1(1)
testPool.explanation: Only category (a) (spouse or civil partner) attracts the fuller standard. The aunt, falling under category (e), is confined to what is reasonable for her maintenance, however genuine her dependency was.

testPool.prompt: Under s 1(2) of the 1975 Act, which phrase distinguishes the spousal standard from every other applicant's standard?
options: 'whether or not that provision is required for his or her maintenance'
'in all the circumstances of the case'
'reasonable financial provision'
'such provision as the court thinks fit'
testPool.explanation: That phrase is what removes the maintenance ceiling for a spouse or civil partner — it is the operative wording that every other applicant's standard lacks.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the categories of eligible applicant listed in s 1(1) of the 1975 Act?
options: Any close relative of the deceased, regardless of maintenance or family treatment
A child of the deceased
A former spouse who has not remarried
A person maintained wholly or partly by the deceased immediately before death
testPool.explanation: There is no free-standing 'close relative' category. Relatives outside the spouse, former spouse, cohabitant, child, and child-of-the-family categories can only claim, if at all, under category (e) by showing they were actually maintained by the deceased.

testPool.prompt: Section 1(1A) of the 1975 Act (defining category (ba)) requires cohabitation for which period?
options: The whole of the two years immediately before the deceased's death
Any continuous period of twelve months during the relationship
The whole of the marriage, however long it lasted
Five years, mirroring the qualifying period for some pension schemes
testPool.explanation: The statutory period is precise: the whole of the two years ending immediately before death, continuously — not any two years at any point in the relationship's history.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap in this lesson is treating eligibility as a matter of impression — closeness, fairness, or how long a relationship lasted — rather than checking the precise statutory category and, separately, which standard of provision that category attracts.
